title: 'Poltergeist' stacked chairs in eerie tower when Most Haunted visited historic house
excerpt: THE butler leading this weekend’s Hallowe’en ghost tours at Kiplin Hall, taking visitors from room to room and telling them centuries of spooky stories, has plenty of material to raise the hairs on the back of the neck.
content:
THE butler leading this weekend’s Hallowe’en ghost tours at Kiplin Hall, taking visitors from room to room and telling them centuries of spooky stories, has plenty of material to raise the hairs on the back of the neck.

This 400-year-old hall, between Northallerton and Scorton, has to be one of the most haunted places in the area with scores and scores of ghosts competing for attention.

Kiplin Hall, between Northallerton and Scorton, is one of the most haunted places in the district (Image: Kiplin Hall)

On the staircase, one of them grabs visitors and moves them towards the bannister. In the Long Gallery, a child’s cold hand has tightly squeezed hold of a passing, living stranger.

There is a woman sobbing in a distant room. There are creaking floorboards and closing doors. There’s a man suffering from painful gout. There’s a butler carrying tea on a silver salver.

In a puff of pipe smoke, there are two RAF officers arguing over a mission that went wrong (Kiplin was requisitioned by the air force in the Second World War).

There’s a vicar in an alcove and Winston Churchill in the drawing room, plus the spirit of Charles II in his own portrait.

There are ghosts with catchphrases. Teddy, a 17th Century stablelad in the back lobby, is so concerned about getting his appearance right that he says: “Buckle shoes on Sunday.”

And in the Green Bedroom, a strong female energy enters, sits on the bed, and says: “Something’s missing. Where’s the cradle?”

Lady Sarah Tyrconnel, who lost her only baby at Kipling Hall in 1847 (Image: Unknown)

Could this be Sarah, Lady Tyrconnel? She was the heiress to the hall who married at 18 but didn’t have any children until, aged 47, she surprised herself on February 19, 1847, by giving birth to a daughter, Lady Elizabeth, who died within hours. It is little wonder that such a rollercoaster of powerful human emotions could have somehow imprinted themselves into the fabric of the Jacobean mansion.

Kiplin Hall, between Northallerton and Scorton, is one of the most haunted places in the district (Image: Kiplin Hall)

And there are shadowy figures beyond the ken of mere mortals but which can scare the living daylights out of visiting dogs and which can fill the frames of digital cameras with moving orbs of invisible energy.

The butler leading the ghost tours at Kiplin Hall, between Northallerton and Scorton (Image: Kiplin Hall)

But it is when the butler on his tour reaches the upper floor that things turn decidedly curious. The education room was, in the 1890s, the governess’ room, and she is seen – prim and proper, dressed in grey – in there.

Investigators reckon there are the spirits of six or seven children in the hall, who have died across the centuries. They complain of sore throats, so perhaps they were the victims of diphtheria, but they play happily together – particularly, it seems, in the education room where for the last 25 years there have been stories of pesky, poltergeist activity.

Kiplin Hall, between Northallerton and Scorton, is one of the most haunted places in the district (Image: Kiplin Hall)

It centres on the child-sized chairs which, at the end of a day, are lifted onto the tables so the floor beneath them can be washed. On several occasions, unknown hands have playfully, and noisily, scattered the chairs back down to the floor.

But then in 2009, the crew of the Most Haunted TV programme visited Kiplin to prepare for filming. This is a programme in which the presenters and producers scare the bejesus out of each other by filming floating orbs, feeling imaginary fingers brush their cheeks and experiencing sudden drops in temperature.

The chairs apparently stacked by a poltergeist in the education room at Kiplin Hall (Image: Kiplin Hall)

When they entered the education room, they found the metal chairs had been strewn in a tangle around the floor, as had happened previously, but the wooden chairs had been stacked neatly onto the table in a strange geometric tower.

Having told this story, and shown the photograph of the tower, the butler will lead the Hallowe’en visitors downstairs and disappear, leaving them wondering if he were a guide or a ghost.

The butler leading the ghost tours at Kiplin Hall, between Northallerton and Scorton (Image: Kiplin Hall)

  • Kiplin’s new ghost tours are tomorrow and Saturday night (Friday, October 30 & Saturday, October 31, 2026) at 5.30pm and 7pm. The tours involve moving around Kiplin Hall in atmospheric low lighting and climbing two staircases. They are not suitable for children under 14, and seasonal refreshments will be available in the café before and after the tour. Booking is essential via the website, kiplinhall.co.uk

St Cuthbert's Church, Kirkleatham, near Redcar, is probably on the site of Thomas de Thweng's chantry (Image: Unknown)

IT is only in modern times that we have come to mark Hallowe’en with ghoulish stories and cheap Chinese tat. In times gone past, this was a season for remembering the dead with bell-ringing and bonfires, and in some parts of the country, with “soulling”, where poor people went from door to door offering prayers for the departed in return for “soul cakes” which were like shortbread biscuits.

We are grateful to Peter Sotheran, of Redcar, for sending a note from his considerable files about how All Hallows’ Eve – the day before All Saints’ Day on November 1 – was marked 700 years ago.

In Kirkleatham, a chantry was established – probably on the site of today’s church dedicated to St Cuthbert – by rector Thomas de Thweng so that 12 priests could pray for the souls of departed members of his family.

These would include his great-grandfather Robert de Thweng, from Thwing near Bridlington, who in 1222 married Matilda de Kilton, the heiress to much of east Cleveland. Robert found popular notoriety under the pseudonym “Will Wither”, leading armed attacks against Italian clergymen who were coming over here and taking jobs from Englishmen.

They also included Thomas’ father, Marmaduke de Thweng, a noted knight who fought for the English at the 1314 Battle of Bannockburn. When he saw the battle was lost, rather than join his countrymen in running away, Marmaduke remained on the battlefield and made his way to the Scottish king, Robert the Bruce, so he could surrender personally.

Robert received him courteously, fed him at his top table and generously released him without demanding a ransom.

Peter Sotheran’s document shows that from 1348, the 12 priests at the new Kirkleatham chantry were to be paid 20 shillings each and given a new cloak. On the “vigil of All Saints”, otherwise known as Hallowe’en, they were to be given a supply of sea coal and 20lbs of candles plus “two flagons of best ale for to drink in their chambers every night”.

However, the priests of Kirkleatham couldn’t spend Hallowe’en getting ghoulishly drunk. A flagon is a large jug, which would hold, say, two pints, and the document says they had to make their beer last until the festival of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary on February 2.
